question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: I would like to tell you about the summer fete we put on in our village two years ago, because it is the best example I have of working with other people towards something we all wanted, and I will try to give you the whole picture. The fete had not run for six years. The old committee had drifted apart, the field had been let to a farmer for grazing and most people assumed it was gone for good. A neighbour and I got talking at the bus stop one morning in February and agreed that somebody ought to bring it back, and by the end of that week there were seven of us round my kitchen table with a pot of tea and a blank sheet of paper. Our goal was simple enough to say out loud: a fete on the second Saturday in July, open to everyone, that at least covered its costs and ideally raised something for the village hall roof. I ended up as secretary, mostly because I own a laptop and nobody else wanted to take the minutes. In practice that meant I kept the list of jobs, chased people when things went quiet and held the one diary that showed who was doing what and by when. We met every other Tuesday, and after each meeting I sent round a single page with the decisions at the top and the open jobs underneath with a name against each, so that nobody had to remember what they had promised. Early on that page was mostly gaps. We had no field, no insurance, no money and no tables. I took on the field myself. I went to see the farmer, listened to his worries about the gate being left open and litter in the grass, and came back with an agreement that we could have it for the weekend provided we stewarded the gate all day and walked the field with bin bags on the Sunday. One of the others, who had run a market stall for years, knew far more than I did about what stallholders expect, so I asked her to look over the booking form I had drafted. She told me, kindly, that it was three times too long and that nobody would pay a deposit in March for a July event they had never heard of. I rewrote it to fit on one side of paper and we dropped the deposit in favour of a small fee on the day, and bookings started coming in within a fortnight. The hardest stretch was in May. Two members of the committee wanted very different things. One wanted a traditional afternoon, with a dog show, a cake competition and a brass band, and felt strongly that many of the long-standing residents would stay away from anything louder. The other wanted a stage with local bands into the evening and a bar, and argued just as strongly that without those we would get few new faces and no money for the roof. It got to the point where they were not replying to each other's messages. I rang each of them separately and asked what mattered most, not what they were against. The first said it was people having somewhere to sit and hear themselves talk. The second said it was the bar takings. So at the next meeting I proposed splitting the day in two. From noon to five the field would be the traditional fete, with the band stand at the far end by the hedge and seating under the trees, and from five the stage would take over, with the bar open from four so the two halves overlapped by an hour. They both agreed to it that evening, a little to their own surprise, and each of them took charge of their own half. In the last month I mainly helped wherever someone was stuck. I spent two evenings painting signs with the couple running the car park, and when our treasurer was ill for a week I counted and banked the stall fees for him and handed the book back the day he returned. On the day itself we had just over nine hundred people through the gate, forty one stalls, and no rain until the bands had finished. We cleared a little over three thousand pounds for the roof after costs. The farmer was happy with the state of the field and offered it again for the following year. The committee kept the one page of jobs and the split day, and both have been used for the two fetes since. What I took from it is that most of what I did was small: writing things down, asking the person who knew more than I did, and getting two people to say what they actually wanted. None of it was clever, but I think it is the reason seven people who barely knew each other in February were still speaking to each other, and still on the committee, the following spring.

question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer: The example I would give is from a night shift when I was the only engineer in the building. The boiler that heats the swimming pool locked out three times before midnight. I read the fault history on the control panel and saw that every lockout followed a low water pressure reading, so I checked the pressure vessel with a gauge and found it had lost its air charge. That explained why the pressure dipped whenever the burner fired. I recharged the vessel with the foot pump, reset the boiler and stood by it through two full firing cycles to see that the pressure held. It ran for the rest of the night without locking out.
